title: The ANTI-Social Network

jokes.text: They blew on their sign until it came off 'cause they thought it was cool?
jokes.setup: Mac explains the bar has no sign because the owners deliberately removed it for cool-factor exclusivity.
jokes.punchline: Charlie interprets this as the owners literally blowing on the sign with their mouths until it came off.
jokes.explanation: Classic Charlie Kelly stupidity — taking something figurative or implied completely literally. The specificity of 'blowing' is funny, and the follow-up confusion is perfectly in character. High character integration because this only works as a Charlie line.

dialogue.line: They blew on their sign until it came off 'cause they thought it was cool?

jokes.text: What the hell is this? Is this water? No, it's gin. Aw! Gin?! I hate gin! Get me a beer!
jokes.setup: The group has entered a hip bar they want to emulate for Paddy's.
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately hates the bar's signature offering and demands a beer like an entitled child.
jokes.explanation: Frank's id-driven reaction is very on-character — he immediately rejects the hip concept they came to study. The escalating outrage ('Aw! Gin?! I hate gin!') is well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: He and his Jews have connected the whole world, and now they're toppling regimes.

jokes.text: It's all connected by Bill Gates and that rain man, Zuckerberg. He and his Jews have connected the whole world, and now they're toppling regimes. And Egypt and Japan and the Jews are all peaceful together...
jokes.setup: The gang discusses Facebook's power to bring people together and grow business.
jokes.punchline: Frank gives a conspiratorial, casually antisemitic, geographically confused rant that is somehow both bigoted AND nonsensical — referencing Egypt and Japan in the same breath as a cohesive political movement.
jokes.explanation: The joke works because it's layered: Frank calls Zuckerberg 'rain man,' casually drops antisemitic conspiracy, then immediately contradicts himself by saying everyone is 'all peaceful together.' It's satire of a certain kind of boomer ignorance — the character is too dumb to even commit to a coherent conspiracy theory. High character integration: only Frank could deliver this.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: And Egypt and Japan and the Jews are all peaceful together...

jokes.text: Dennis's diplomatic pivot: 'I understand the spirit of what you're saying... Facebook is connecting everyone these days. Even people in the Middle East.'
jokes.setup: Frank has just delivered a bigoted, confused rant about Zuckerberg and Jews toppling regimes.
jokes.punchline: Dennis smoothly translates the insane rant into polite business-speak, as if 'that's what I'm talking about' is a reasonable response to what Frank said.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's ability to diplomatically re-interpret Frank's insanity is a recurring group dynamic joke that works here with economy and precision. The gap between what Frank said and Dennis's sanitized version is the entire joke.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Do you think a human being can blow a sign off of a building? I didn't until Mac said it.

jokes.text: We have to get rid of all the beer in Paddy's. We have to blow the sign off of the building — you know, maybe I'll do the blowing, that's fine.
jokes.setup: The gang is discussing how to emulate the hip gin bar's model.
jokes.punchline: Mac, who explicitly denied anyone could blow a sign off a building moments earlier, now volunteers to do the blowing — having been slowly convinced by Charlie's idiot logic.
jokes.explanation: This is a tight callback with real payoff — Mac explicitly refuted the sign-blowing theory and now has absorbed it and volunteered for the job. The 'that's fine' casualness is perfect character voice. Good structural comedy: the callback has changed Mac's position, which is the escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: In Charlie's defense, you could loosen the screws, get up there and blow...

jokes.text: Charlie, Charlie, stop, stop, stop — do you think a human being can blow a sign off of a building? I didn't until Mac said it. I never said that!
jokes.setup: Mac tries to refute the sign-blowing theory again.
jokes.punchline: Charlie confirms Mac is the source of the sign-blowing idea; Mac furiously denies it — but he literally just said it.
jokes.explanation: The three-way rapid exchange is well-structured. Mac denying something he said 15 seconds ago is a tightly paced joke about self-delusion, a core Mac trait.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Ugh. Ew. What the hell was that?

jokes.text: In Charlie's defense, you could loosen the screws, get up there and blow...
jokes.setup: Dennis tells Charlie to stop the sign-blowing tangent.
jokes.punchline: Mac, now firmly on Team Sign-Blowing, offers a technical workaround — loosen the screws, then blow.
jokes.explanation: Mac can't help himself — his need to seem smart leads him to propose a 'technical' solution to the absurd premise. This extends the sign-blowing gag with a natural escalation and is very Mac.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: We'll do a really cool video of how we serve gin in spaghetti cans or something like that.

jokes.text: Ugh. Ew. What the hell was that? Okay, don't worry about it, okay.
jokes.setup: The group is at the gin bar, supposedly having a business discussion.
jokes.punchline: Something disgusting/awkward happens that is not explained — a reaction beat to an unseen physical event (likely Dee tasting the gin or a bar patron doing something gross). Mac shuts it down immediately.
jokes.explanation: Classic IASIP unexplained reaction beat — something visually horrible happens and the group refuses to engage with it. Works better visually than it reads in transcript, hence the rewatch bonus.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I got the sign down. And there's no way a man could have blown that off of our bar.

jokes.text: We could do a viral video for Paddy's. We'll do a really cool video of how we serve gin in spaghetti cans or something like that. And we take the sign down.
jokes.setup: The gang is brainstorming how to emulate the hip bar's web presence.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's idea of a 'cool viral video' is serving gin in spaghetti cans, and Frank is still fixated on removing the sign — both completely missing the point of viral marketing.
jokes.explanation: 'Gin in spaghetti cans' is a beautifully specific absurd detail that only Charlie would generate. Frank's continued sign fixation extends the running gag. Both characters are consistent in their idiocy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I never once said that!

jokes.text: What kind of a douchebag walks into a bar just because it doesn't have a sign outside of it? That's stupid, Frank. Use your head.
jokes.setup: Frank insists exclusivity (weird drinks, no sign) is the key to the gin bar's success.
jokes.punchline: Mac mocks the idea as stupid — but they are literally standing in the gin bar, having come specifically because it was cool and had no sign.
jokes.explanation: Classic dramatic irony — the character is completely unaware of his own hypocrisy. Mac has zero self-awareness, which is a defining trait. The joke is tight and self-contained.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: The guy that shushed us last night-- is that bugging anybody else?

jokes.text: I got the sign down.
jokes.setup: The gang is debating whether to remove Paddy's sign as part of their new marketing strategy.
jokes.punchline: While everyone was arguing, Charlie went and physically removed the sign — apparently mid-conversation — proving he has been taking the sign-blowing theory seriously all along.
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum impact. This is excellent sitcom writing — the entire sign-blowing runner pays off with Charlie having silently acted on his absurd literal interpretation while everyone else was arguing. The economy is perfect (10/10 — could not be shorter). The callback rewards audience attention. It's entirely in character: Charlie does things, he doesn't just talk about them. This is the sign-blowing gag's apex.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I don't shush them like they're animals. I use my words.

jokes.text: And there's no way a man could have blown that off of our bar. There's just no way. You're totally wrong about that, Mac.
jokes.setup: Charlie announces he got the sign down. Mac continues to insist a human can't blow a sign off a building.
jokes.punchline: Charlie (and implicitly the audience) knows the sign IS down — Mac's denial is now comically irrelevant.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in Mac's continued denial despite evidence to the contrary. Charlie's calm 'you're totally wrong about that, Mac' is quietly funny coming from the person who just physically did the thing in question.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: And we'll pop a shush on the guy and we'll be right back.

jokes.text: The guy that shushed us last night — is that bugging anybody else? I've been thinking about that, too.
jokes.setup: The gang is mid-discussion about their important viral marketing strategy.
jokes.punchline: Dennis derails everything to bring up being shushed at the bar — a completely trivial slight that he has clearly been stewing over. Mac immediately validates it.
jokes.explanation: This is the inciting incident for the episode's main plot — the gang's narcissism means a minor social slight completely derails their legitimate business plan. The two of them bonding over this like it's serious is very funny and character-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Facebook. Found him.

jokes.text: I was telling him to be quiet, I was telling him to be quiet. I tell everybody to be quiet. I don't shush them like they're animals. I use my words.
jokes.setup: Mac points out Dennis was doing the same thing (telling Charlie to be quiet) as the shusher.
jokes.punchline: Dennis draws a sharp distinction between 'using words' and shushing — but the distinction is entirely self-serving and absurd given he was doing the same thing.
jokes.explanation: This is a tight Dennis joke — his narcissism means the same behavior is dignified when he does it and monstrous when others do it. 'I use my words' is the punchline and it's very quotable. High character integration: this is a pure Dennis Reynolds moment.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: What if you hit it faster?

jokes.text: We'll pop a shush on the guy and we'll be right back.
jokes.setup: The gang nominally wants to do the viral video but can't let the shushing go.
jokes.punchline: Mac describes their revenge plan with cheerful, casual confidence — 'pop a shush on the guy' — as if this is a normal and achievable errand.
jokes.explanation: 'Pop a shush on the guy' is a funny phrase — the casual violence implied by 'pop' applied to such a minor act. Economical and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: for all this guy knows, I'm a psychopath with a trunk full of chainsaws, right?

jokes.text: You can just find the guy on Facebook. That's where you find people these days. You aren't gonna find the guy on Facebook. There's three billion people on there. Are you crazy? ... Facebook. Found him.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis dismiss Dee's suggestion to find the shusher on Facebook as naive.
jokes.punchline: Within seconds, Charlie finds the shusher on Facebook — he was friends with the Gin Bar page.
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic structure: confident dismissal immediately undercut by reality. The economy is excellent — the buildup of skepticism ('three billion people') makes the instant payoff ('Found him.') very satisfying. 'Facebook. Found him.' as a two-word punchline after a speech about impossibility is tight writing.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: And I could be a man with a fist full of hammers... and a trunk full of duct tape and zip ties.

jokes.text: Maybe we can just, you know, send him a friend request and then... see if he responds. And then we'll get back to what we were doing.
jokes.setup: The gang has found the shusher on Facebook and can now pursue the shush-revenge plan.
jokes.punchline: Their 'plan' degrades to just sending a friend request to their enemy and waiting — still pretending they'll get back to the viral video eventually.
jokes.explanation: Functional joke about the gang's total inability to stay on task. The 'friend request to an enemy' idea is mildly absurd. Not a standout but moves the plot.

dialogue.line: Yeah, people who could have chainsaws. Or hammers.

jokes.text: Refresh. No. What if you hit it faster?
jokes.setup: The gang is waiting for the shusher to accept their friend request.
jokes.punchline: Charlie asks 'what if you hit it faster?' — genuinely believing that clicking refresh faster will make the response come faster.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical Charlie stupidity — 'what if you hit it faster?' encapsulates his magical thinking about technology in five words. High character integration and economy. Quotable in everyday internet-usage contexts.

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: Don't think I'd care.

jokes.text: Tweeting — that's not having a conversation. What is that? ...and they hear you having a real conversation with your real buddies, your real pals, and they get all jealous and pissed off and they want to shush you.
jokes.setup: Dennis is ranting against social media disconnection.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's earnest speech about 'real connection' is completely self-serving — he's rationalizing being angry at a stranger for the crime of shushing him in public.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's ability to construct elaborate self-justifications for petty grievances is core to his character. The logic here — people shush you because they're jealous of your 'real' friendships — is hilariously grandiose.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Shh!

jokes.text: For all this guy knows, I'm a psychopath with a trunk full of chainsaws, right? He shushes me 'cause he doesn't like the volume of my conversation? Next thing he knows he's chopped to bits in a basement somewhere, you know? Was that worth it?
jokes.setup: Charlie is expressing outrage at being shushed by a stranger.
jokes.punchline: Charlie's defense of his right not to be shushed is that the shusher should have considered that Charlie might be a chainsaw murderer — framing serial killer potential as a valid social courtesy argument.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The logic is perfect: Charlie's argument for why shushing is rude is that the shusher didn't account for the possibility that Charlie is a murderer. 'Was that worth it?' as the closing question is a great button — delivered as genuine advice. It's dark, specific, and reveals Charlie's unhinged worldview with wonderful economy. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in its originality and character specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: I mean, I was finished speaking.

jokes.text: And I could be a man with a fist full of hammers... and a trunk full of duct tape and zip ties. You know, this guy doesn't know me. Is he crazy?
jokes.setup: Charlie has established the chainsaw-murderer argument. Mac continues the thought.
jokes.punchline: Mac contributes his own murder-kit inventory (hammers, duct tape, zip ties) to the argument, escalating the specific threat with equally horrifying specificity.
jokes.explanation: Mac escalating the murder inventory is a perfect escalation beat — the specificity of 'fist full of hammers' and 'duct tape and zip ties' makes it funnier than just generic violence. Each character contributes their own murder kit, which is a great running escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: It's like an online shush.

jokes.text: It's very upsetting to me that he didn't consider any of that.
jokes.setup: Charlie and Mac have outlined their potential as murderers as an argument against being shushed.
jokes.punchline: Charlie closes the argument with earnest disappointment that the shusher failed to consider their murder potential — delivered as genuine hurt feelings.
jokes.explanation: The button on the murder-kit sequence. 'Very upsetting to me' in the context of his own potential for violence is the perfect understatement button. Economy is excellent — this five-word sentence closes out a great comedic escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Say, 'I got infected.'

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Get that away from me.

jokes.text: This is a rude man, and they are very seldom the same people.
jokes.setup: Mac is agreeing that the shusher is not a considerate man.
jokes.punchline: Mac delivers the pseudo-profound observation 'rude men and considerate men are very seldom the same people' — a tautology stated as wisdom.
jokes.explanation: Mac delivers a tautology ('rude men are rarely the same as considerate men') as if it's a profound insight. This is a classic IASIP move — characters speaking with authority while saying nothing. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Dylan Toback
dialogue.line: I am a man-whore. I hate women. I am a liar.

jokes.text: Yeah, people who could have chainsaws. Or hammers.
jokes.setup: The gang is describing the shusher to a bartender.
jokes.punchline: Charlie and Mac add their murder-kit items to the description of why the shushing was dangerous — still making the case that the shusher should have considered their homicidal potential.
jokes.explanation: Keeps the murder-kit callback alive in a new setting. The bartender's confusion makes this land — the audience has context the bartender doesn't.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: A silk sash at Tootie's?

jokes.text: I don't see what the big deal is. / The big deal, sir, is that a grown man shushed me and my friend here. We demand satisfaction from this person.
jokes.setup: Dennis is explaining their grievance to the bartender.
jokes.punchline: Dennis escalates 'we demand satisfaction' — formal, dueling-code language — over being shushed at a bar.
jokes.explanation: 'We demand satisfaction' applied to a shushing incident is a great Dennis line — he lives in a world of grandiose self-importance. Character integration is high.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Daddy got a new plan.

jokes.text: Look, how would you like to be shushed? Don't think I'd care. Shh! How'd that feel? I mean, I was finished speaking.
jokes.setup: Dennis asks the bartender how he'd feel about being shushed, to make a point.
jokes.punchline: The bartender says he wouldn't care; Dennis shushes him anyway; the bartender points out he was done talking — completely defusing the demonstration.
jokes.explanation: The shushing demonstration is undermined because the bartender was already done speaking — making the shush meaningless. The structure is tight: Dennis sets up a demonstration, it immediately fails, and he has to try again. The bartender's flat 'I mean, I was finished speaking' is a perfect straight-man response.

dialogue.line: Yeah, well, yeah... He was raping us... Well... wha...? He was raping you. Yeah, well, yeah...

jokes.text: Well, shh to you! / Again, I was done, so... / You're speaking too fast. Stop speaking in such short sentences. Then we can shush you in the middle and you'll know how it feels.
jokes.setup: Dennis's shushing demonstration failed because the bartender spoke in short sentences.
jokes.punchline: Mac's solution: demand the bartender speak in longer sentences so they can shush him mid-sentence — an increasingly absurd negotiation about the terms of a demonstration shush.
jokes.explanation: The escalating negotiation over how to properly shush the bartender is very funny — the gang is so committed to making a point about shushing that they create increasingly elaborate rules. This is IASIP at its cringe best.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No. You can't rape two guys.

jokes.text: Do you guys want a drink, or what? Yeah. Yeah, we want drinks. Absolutely. Okay, two house specials? Shh! Specials, yeah. Got interrupted. How'd that feel?
jokes.setup: The bartender tries to move on and take their order.
jokes.punchline: Dennis and Mac shush the bartender mid-order, then ask 'how'd that feel?' — having finally successfully executed a mid-sentence shush, they're triumphant.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the shushing demonstration sequence — after multiple failed attempts, they finally land a shush mid-sentence during the drink order. 'Got interrupted. How'd that feel?' is a satisfying button. The bartender's resignation is implied and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: The guy never quite made it inside of me but, my friend here, yeah... He, like, really, kinda made soup of your insides...

jokes.text: On your way. I think you got him with that one, though. I don't exactly feel good about it. No. But he had to know how it feels.
jokes.setup: After successfully shushing the bartender mid-order.
jokes.punchline: Dennis admits he doesn't feel good about shushing the bartender — the moral cost of their petty revenge has begun to weigh on him.
jokes.explanation: Mild beat — Dennis's unexpected moral qualm after shushing is a small character note. Functional but not standout.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: And the guy was super-small, so I'm fine.

jokes.text: Refresh. Goddamn it. Why won't this guy be our friend? It's like an online shush.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are still waiting for the shusher to accept their Facebook friend request.
jokes.punchline: Mac invents the concept of an 'online shush' — interpreting the lack of a friend request response as a digital act of rudeness equivalent to the original shush.
jokes.explanation: 'It's like an online shush' is a great coinage — it perfectly captures Mac's grievance and extends the shushing metaphor to the digital world in a way that's specific and quotable. High economy and quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: That's him.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: That is him.

jokes.text: Paddy's Pub has over 30 friends at this point.
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to frame Paddy's social media presence positively.
jokes.punchline: 30 friends is presented as an accomplishment — a pathetically low number that Mac is genuinely proud of.
jokes.explanation: Quick joke about Paddy's irrelevance. Mac's pride in 30 Facebook friends is a small but effective beat about the bar's pathetic status.

dialogue.line: Sorry about that, ma'am. Hi, ma'am. Uh, we thought you were this guy, Dylan Toback.

jokes.text: Oh! We got him! We got you, Dylan Toback! You giant douche!
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis find Dylan Toback's Facebook profile.
jokes.punchline: They address the profile photo directly and triumphantly as if Dylan can hear them.
jokes.explanation: Mild joke about their excitement being disproportionate. Finding someone on Facebook is not the victory they think it is. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I did because of your hair. Here's why: it's the hair and it's the cardigan, and it's the build... It's the way you stand, and the broad shoulders.

jokes.text: Are you guys gonna help me do the virus thing, or what?
jokes.setup: Frank has been dutifully filming the virus video while everyone ignores him.
jokes.punchline: Frank's plaintive question — after everyone has completely abandoned the viral video project they said was the most important thing — is a perfect expression of the gang's flakiness.
jokes.explanation: Frank as the abandoned man who's doing the actual work while the gang chases trivia is a good character moment. His plaintive 'or what?' captures Frank's combination of frustration and low expectations.

dialogue.speaker: Dylan
dialogue.line: Sally, send me money.

dialogue.speaker: Dylan
dialogue.line: Sally, mail me hair.

jokes.text: No, no! We said the viral video is very important, and it is very important — but we're on to this now. You know, we'll do it later. Why don't you get it started and then we'll come and fix what you did, okay?
jokes.setup: Frank points out they said the viral video was most important.
jokes.punchline: Mac both affirms the viral video's importance AND dismisses it, then tells Frank to start it so they can 'fix what he did' — a stunning pre-failure of confidence.
jokes.explanation: 'We'll come and fix what you did' is the best part — Mac is confident Frank will screw it up before he's even started. This foreshadows the virus video payoff and is a great character note about the gang's fractured trust.

dialogue.speaker: Sally
dialogue.line: Mail him hair? Weird, right?

jokes.text: Oh, check out these updates: 'I am a man-whore. I hate women. I am a liar.' He admits that he is a liar. Son of a bitch!
jokes.setup: Dennis is reading Dylan Toback's Facebook status updates aloud.
jokes.punchline: The updates are suspiciously confessional ('I am a man-whore, I hate women, I am a liar') and Dennis treats them as genuine admissions, particularly scandalized that 'he admits to being a liar.'
jokes.explanation: The fact that someone would post 'I am a liar' as a status update — and Dennis being specifically outraged by that one — is funny. This also foreshadows that the Facebook persona is fake, which pays off later. Good layered writing.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Aw, those disgusting ex-girlfriend porno sites! I mean, there's so many of them, though! Which one?

jokes.text: A silk sash at Tootie's? What an asshole.
jokes.setup: Dennis reads that Dylan Toback posted he's shopping for a silk sash.
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately judges him as an asshole for the silk sash — both the specificity of 'silk sash' and Mac's instant moral condemnation are the joke.
jokes.explanation: 'A silk sash at Tootie's? What an asshole.' is efficiently funny — the specificity of 'silk sash' and 'Tootie's' and the complete confidence of the character judgment. Good economy.

jokes.text: Daddy got a new plan. Mm-hmm. Daddy got a new plan. Let's head down to Tootie's and we'll fire a shush right in his face.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis know where Dylan Toback is.
jokes.punchline: Mac refers to himself as 'Daddy' and describes their plan to 'fire a shush right in his face' — both the self-designation and the violent framing of a shush as aggression.
jokes.explanation: 'Daddy got a new plan' is a funny self-designation — Mac's bizarre paternal authority complex. 'Fire a shush right in his face' frames the shush as a violent act, which is the episode's central comic conceit executed well.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: This chick is douchier than Dylan. Let's get outta here!

jokes.text: But we won't tell Dennis and Charlie, 'cause they mocked us. Eventually, we'll tell them, though, right? Well, we won't tell them right now, but we'll come back and we'll jam it in their faces.
jokes.setup: Mac and Frank are planning to find the shusher without telling the others.
jokes.punchline: Their plan to withhold news has two stated phases: (1) don't tell them now, (2) 'jam it in their faces' later — the pettiness is the joke.
jokes.explanation: 'Jam it in their faces' as the stated end goal of a plan reveals the gang's pettiness hierarchy — even their victories are primarily for one-upmanship. Good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'm going to write 'Rude man who shushes, please call' at the top, and then, at the bottom, I'll put my phone number.

jokes.text: I want to make sure you got the nose right, though. That's the most important part to me, because it was an annoying nose. It was a nose that you wanted to smack, yeah.
jokes.setup: Dennis and Charlie are at the police station having a sketch artist draw the shusher.
jokes.punchline: Mac is deeply invested in the nose — describes it as 'a nose you wanted to smack' — a very specific and human grievance that reveals how thoroughly he has internalized this grudge.
jokes.explanation: 'A nose you wanted to smack' is a great specific detail — this kind of visceral, petty character observation is classic Dennis/Mac. It makes the grudge feel real and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I'm saying call me, let's have a phone conversation. Yeah, don't tweet. Don't just tweet me, don't shush me-- you know, let's connect.

jokes.text: Mr. Reynolds, Mr. Kelly, I'm Detective Larson. I'm gonna need to clear something up on your report here. It says here this was filed as an assault, but the only thing you're claiming was that this man shushed you? Yeah. But it was an assault.
jokes.setup: Dennis and Charlie have filed a police report describing their shushing as an assault.
jokes.punchline: The detective expresses incredulity; Dennis confirms — yes, being shushed is an assault — with complete confidence.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that they've filed a police report about a shushing is a perfect escalation of the episode's central premise. The detective's flat confusion and Dennis's confident 'it was an assault' plays the irony well.

dialogue.speaker: Catfish
dialogue.line: I am Dylan Toback.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No, no, no... Mm-mm, mm-mm, mm-mm... Don't say that!

jokes.text: And the reason it was an assault was because he was shushing our cries for help. Right. This guy was raping us...
jokes.setup: Detective asks why they're calling it assault when only a shush occurred.
jokes.punchline: Charlie invents a rape narrative to justify the assault charge — escalating from shushing to rape in one sentence.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's willingness to invent a rape narrative on the spot — and Dennis's immediate participation — is classic IASIP dark escalation. The characters' moral flexibility is the joke. The improv nature of the lie (they're clearly making it up as they go) makes it funnier.

dialogue.line: My real name is Catfish!

jokes.text: I wouldn't even necessarily classify it... You know what happened was that he only raped my friend here. I actually shook him off in time. The guy never quite made it inside of me but, my friend here, yeah...
jokes.setup: Dennis and Charlie are elaborating on their fake rape narrative.
jokes.punchline: Dennis adds a personal detail — he 'shook him off in time' — implying near-penetration, then pivots to throwing Charlie fully under the bus as the 'actual' rape victim.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's self-serving version of events — he 'got away' while Charlie is the full victim — is a perfect character note. His willingness to sacrifice Charlie while also boasting about his own near-escape is exactly the kind of narcissistic self-preservation that defines Dennis. The escalating specificity is very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Don't you shush me! Don't you shush us, goddamn it. Don't disturb Jerry.

jokes.text: Yeah, but he bit his dick. Not-- what?! / He did... the reason we were going to file as a rape was because he did make it inside me, but, like, just barely. And the guy was super-small, so I'm fine.
jokes.setup: Dennis has claimed he wasn't fully raped; Charlie corrects the story.
jokes.punchline: Charlie tries to rehabilitate Dennis's story ('he bit his dick'), then Dennis adds a qualifier — 'just barely' made it, 'super-small,' so he's fine — a horrifying set of specifics.
jokes.explanation: The escalation continues with Dennis revising his story downward — 'just barely, super-small, so I'm fine' — which creates a bizarre reassurance that only makes it worse. The detective's growing horror is implied and essential. This sequence is a masterclass in IASIP's escalating dark comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Dee banged a fat old black lady, and then sent her hair.

jokes.text: Look, can we just drop the case? Yeah! Right? We don't need to... Just need the drawing... this never needs to go in any files anywhere.
jokes.setup: After inventing an elaborate false rape narrative to escalate their police report.
jokes.punchline: Now that it's on record, they just want to quietly drop it and get the sketch — the entire false report was for the purpose of getting a free police sketch.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that the whole fake rape narrative was an attempt to access police sketch resources is a good button on the sequence. Their casual 'this never needs to go in any files anywhere' is very IASIP.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Welcome to Paddy's Pub... the oldest pub in America.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Well, that's not true.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Right. No, I lied.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Everybody lies on the Internet.

jokes.text: I got another plan. / [They present a child's crayon drawing of the shusher in a dune buggy with a propeller on his head, shushing]
jokes.setup: The detective won't give them the police sketch because they filed a false report.
jokes.punchline: Charlie has made his own drawing — described as the man in a dune buggy with a propeller on his head, clearly a child-level crayon drawing.
jokes.explanation: Charlie's self-made drawing — which the group immediately praises as 'perfect' and 'looks exactly like him' despite depicting him in a dune buggy with a propeller hat — is a visual gem. High character integration: Charlie's illiteracy and limited artistic ability are established traits. The gap between their effusive praise and the clearly absurd drawing is the joke. 'He wasn't in a dune buggy' said earnestly is a perfect line.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: 'Cause we also got donkey shows, Motley Crue and cake.

jokes.text: That's perfect. That looks exactly like him! Yeah, I mean, he wasn't in a dune buggy and he didn't have a propeller on his head, like that, but... I like the shushing, though. You nailed the shushing!
jokes.setup: Charlie presents his crayon drawing.
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis praise the drawing effusively, then immediately note it's entirely wrong (wrong vehicle, wrong headgear), but praise the shushing gesture — the one correct element of this unusable portrait.
jokes.explanation: 'You nailed the shushing!' after cataloguing everything else that's wrong is a perfect button. The gang's willingness to call an obviously useless drawing 'perfect' because one tiny element is right is very funny and very them.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I am a doctor... Dr. Toboggan. Mantis Toboggan.

jokes.text: Hey, Dylan Toback. Oh! Hey. Sorry about that, ma'am. Hi, ma'am.
jokes.setup: Mac and Frank confront who they think is Dylan Toback at Tootie's.
jokes.punchline: The person they aggressively confront turns out to be a woman — visual gag where Mac physically grabs a woman thinking she was a man.
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection — the reveal that Dylan Toback is a woman (or someone they mistook for a man) is a physical comedy moment. Works better visually than on the page.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I said a 'viral video,' Frank. Goddamn it. Goddamn it!

jokes.text: We didn't think you were a man, per se... I did. Okay, I did, too. I did because of your hair. Here's why: it's the hair and it's the cardigan, and it's the build... It's the way you stand, and the broad shoulders. But that's okay. That's okay. There's nothing you can do about that. Have a nice day.
jokes.setup: Mac and Frank realize they've accosted a woman.
jokes.punchline: Instead of a quick apology, they launch into a detailed catalog of why she looks like a man — hair, cardigan, build, posture, 'broad shoulders' — capped with 'there's nothing you can do about that.'
jokes.explanation: This is excellent cringe comedy. The characters don't apologize — they justify and enumerate. 'There's nothing you can do about that' as a final consolation is devastating. The escalating list of masculine attributes followed by the patronizing dismissal 'have a nice day' is very funny and very IASIP.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: You guys open?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yes, we are. Charlie, lock the door.

jokes.text: Are you guys looking for Dylan Toback? Yeah. He posted on Facebook that he was here. Well, can you guys keep a secret? No! Yes. Yes. Yes, I can... yes, yes. Yes, yes.
jokes.setup: A woman offers to tell them information about Dylan Toback if they can keep a secret.
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately says 'No!' — honest self-assessment — while Mac scrambles to override him with desperate yeses.
jokes.explanation: Frank's immediate and honest 'No!' is the best beat — he's correctly self-assessing their ability to keep secrets. Mac's frantic overrides make it funnier. Good economy.

jokes.text: He was always, like, 'Sally, send me money.' 'Sally, mail me hair.' / Mail him hair? / Weird, right?
jokes.setup: Sally describes her toxic online relationship with Dylan Toback.
jokes.punchline: 'Mail me hair' as an abuse demand — a request so specific and strange it transcends normal relationship toxicity.
jokes.explanation: 'Mail me hair' is the best three words in the episode — an absurd specific demand that immediately signals something deeply wrong with this relationship. 'Weird, right?' as a straight follow-up is perfect. Very quotable and highly original. This becomes important later when Dee has actually mailed hair.

jokes.text: Naked pics online? Where? Where did he post those? / I don't know. One of those disgusting ex-girlfriend porno sites. / Aw, those disgusting ex-girlfriend porno sites! I mean, there's so many of them, though! Which one? Which one did he post it on?
jokes.setup: Sally reveals that Dylan Toback posted nude photos of her on revenge porn sites.
jokes.punchline: Mac and Frank express performative disgust at 'those disgusting sites' while simultaneously and urgently asking which one — their prurient interest completely exposed.
jokes.explanation: The hypocrisy is perfectly executed: they perform outrage ('Aw, those disgusting sites!') immediately followed by 'Which one?' The irony is so thin it's transparent, which is exactly the joke. 'There's so many of them, though!' reveals their familiarity with the genre. High character integration — both Mac and Frank would behave exactly this way.

jokes.text: Well, the pics I sent were a little more flattering than I actually am, and so we just sort of had this online relationship.
jokes.setup: Sally explains she wants to come and get revenge on Dylan because he's never met her in person.
jokes.punchline: The reveal that Sally catfished him with better photos — and they had an 'online relationship' based on a false image — deepens the absurdity of the situation.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the catfishing revelations. Functional rather than a standout joke on its own.

jokes.text: But the hair I mailed was mine. That was real.
jokes.setup: Sally has revealed the relationship was partially fake (flattering photos).
jokes.punchline: In the midst of admitting to deception, Sally insists that the mailed hair was genuine — as if this is the important thing to establish as authentic.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best lines. After revealing she sent false pictures, Sally's urgent clarification that 'the hair I mailed was mine, that was real' is a perfect absurdist button. The logic — lies about appearance are acceptable, but hair authenticity is a point of pride — is completely insane and yet Sally delivers it with earnest sincerity. Economy is near-perfect (nine words). This line is quotable in a way that travels far beyond the episode's context.

jokes.text: Okay, you know what? This chick is douchier than Dylan. Let's get outta here!
jokes.setup: Sally has just revealed she catfished Dylan and mailed him her actual hair.
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately morally positions Sally above Dylan on the douchery scale and announces they're leaving — the gang has a consistent hierarchy of douchery they apply.
jokes.explanation: Mac's snap judgment and immediate exit is very Mac. The gang moving on from an inconvenient truth is a consistent comedy beat. 'Douchier than Dylan' as a comparative moral judgment is a funny formulation.

jokes.text: No, I'm not even gonna look for those nude photos. I might. I might, though. I might.
jokes.setup: Mac declares he won't look for the revenge porn photos.
jokes.punchline: Frank immediately hedges ('I might'), then Mac quickly adds he also might — their moral resolve lasting about two seconds.
jokes.explanation: The repeated 'I might' — with Mac and Frank each admitting their intent with no shame — is funny. The rhythm of 'No... I might. I might, though. I might.' is well-constructed as three beats of declining moral certainty.

jokes.text: I'm sorry, guys, I've never seen a cartoon character in here shushing people before. Well, he wasn't in a dune buggy, he was... Look, use your imagination.
jokes.setup: Dennis and Charlie are showing the bartender Charlie's crayon drawing to identify the shusher.
jokes.punchline: The bartender calls it a 'cartoon character' — confirming the drawing is useless as an ID tool — and Charlie earnestly defends it by saying 'he wasn't in a dune buggy.'
jokes.explanation: The drawing callback lands well with the bartender's reaction. 'Use your imagination' as a request to identify a person from a cartoon is very funny and Charlie-specific.

jokes.text: Here's what I'm gonna do, Charlie. I'm going to write 'Rude man who shushes, please call' at the top, and then, at the bottom, I'll put my phone number. Right? And then we'll make a shitload of copies, we'll put them up all over town, and it'll act like a wanted poster.
jokes.setup: The gang can't identify the shusher through normal means.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's plan to make wanted posters featuring Charlie's crayon drawing and his personal phone number, inviting the rude man to call him — is a completely impractical plan executed with total confidence.
jokes.explanation: The 'wanted poster' plan is a good escalation — taking an escalating trivial grievance to escalating escalatory measures. The detail of putting his personal phone number on a poster distributed across the city foreshadows the prank calls.

jokes.text: So you want the rude man to call you? No, I want people to call me about the rude man. But, if the rude man calls me that works, too. That works, too!
jokes.setup: Charlie questions the logic of the wanted poster plan.
jokes.punchline: Dennis clarifies the poster is for people to call about the rude man — but admits that the rude man calling directly also works, which Charlie eagerly endorses.
jokes.explanation: Charlie accidentally reveals a logic gap in the plan, and Dennis's backup position ('if the rude man calls, that works too') is a funny capitulation. The mutual 'That works, too!' enthusiasm is good.

jokes.text: Now, hold on a second — you're cool just putting your personal information out there? Yeah! I'm absolutely cool with that, man, because I'm saying 'connect with me.' ... call me, let's have a phone conversation... Don't just tweet me, don't shush me — you know, let's connect.
jokes.setup: The episode's theme of internet connection vs. real connection.
jokes.punchline: Dennis connects his anti-social-media screed to putting his personal phone number on thousands of flyers — not seeing any contradiction between advocating for genuine connection and distributing his digits to the entire city.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's self-delusion — thinking mass-distributed personal info is genuine connection — ties the episode's themes together while being funny. His anti-tweet stance while making a public bulletin is well-observed irony.

jokes.text: Sending nude pictures of yourself? That's just stupid, and that's desperate. Yeah, and hair?! I mean, sending hair — that's just demented.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are judging Sally's behavior in her online relationship.
jokes.punchline: Mac is disgusted by nude photos (despite having just asked which site they were on), and Dennis calls sending hair 'demented.'
jokes.explanation: Mac condemning nude photos after urgently asking which site they were on is good irony. The hair judgment pays off the earlier 'mail me hair' absurdity. Rewatch bonus because we know Dee has mailed hair, which makes this judgment funnier in context.

jokes.text: Well, the hair I don't really have a problem with. What are you talking about? What is the point of that? You send your hair to a guy and, you know, you just give that guy a sense of you and your smells... and... you know...
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are judging the hair-mailing as demented.
jokes.punchline: Charlie defends hair-mailing with earnest logic: you send hair so someone can get 'a sense of you and your smells.' He understands and endorses the hair-mailing impulse.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best character jokes. Charlie's earnest defense of hair-mailing — 'a sense of you and your smells' — reveals he would do exactly this and thinks it's a reasonable gesture of intimacy. The trailing '...and... you know...' implies depths of hair-related romance logic he can't fully articulate. Near-perfect character integration: this is 100% a Charlie Kelly worldview. This pays off beautifully when we learn Dee mailed hair to the catfish.

jokes.text: Oh, Lord... I knew this day would come. / Um... come in.
jokes.setup: Mac and Frank knock on what they think is Dylan Toback's door.
jokes.punchline: The door is answered by an elderly woman who says 'I knew this day would come' — implying she has been anticipating consequences for her online activities.
jokes.explanation: The setup of a guilty conscience answering the door is a great misdirection. 'I knew this day would come' suggests she's been living in anticipation of exposure — a funny note of genuine self-awareness from a character who is about to be revealed as a master catfisher.

jokes.text: Speed up, speed up, speed up! / ...ever since Jerry got put on life support — / Whoa! Slow down, slow down, slow down! Ew! I didn't see him there.
jokes.setup: The older woman begins a lengthy explanation. Mac keeps interrupting to manage the pace.
jokes.punchline: She mentions Jerry on life support; Frank reacts to seeing Jerry on life support in the room — presumably a person attached to machines that Frank literally didn't see.
jokes.explanation: The reveal of a person on life support in the room — noticed late by Frank with an 'Ew!' — is dark comedy done efficiently. Mac frantically managing the conversation's pace ('speed up/slow down') is funny, and the life support reveal is unexpected and very IASIP.

jokes.text: Um... I am Dylan Toback. / No, no, no... Mm-mm, mm-mm, mm-mm... Don't say that! / We don't have time for that, okay? Is anybody online the person who they say that they are?
jokes.setup: Mac asks if the woman knows Dylan Toback.
jokes.punchline: The elderly woman declares she IS Dylan Toback; Mac and Frank refuse to accept this — they can't process it; Frank delivers an increasingly exasperated thematic statement about online identity.
jokes.explanation: 'Is anybody online the person who they say that they are?' is a good thematic button delivered by Frank with genuine exasperation. Mac's refusal to accept the information ('Don't say that!') is very Mac — he can't update his mental model.

jokes.text: I've made up dozens of names. I'm really good at it. My real name is Catfish!
jokes.setup: The woman explains she invented the Dylan Toback persona.
jokes.punchline: She reveals her real name is Catfish — she is so deep into online persona creation that her 'real' name is itself a name that describes the act of deceptive online identity.
jokes.explanation: My real name is Catfish!' is a fantastic joke. The woman has so fully embraced her catfishing lifestyle that her identity is the word for the deceptive act. It's layered: is 'Catfish' a nickname she gave herself, a name given to her by others, or a genuinely bizarre given name? Any interpretation is funny. Very quotable and original. This is one of the episode's standout moments.

jokes.text: Here's what I gather. I think she went on the Gin Bar's Web site, found a picture of that guy and then made up a whole name and personality for him. So we don't know the guy's name. No. We don't even know if he's on Facebook. Nope.
jokes.setup: Mac tries to untangle the catfishing revelations.
jokes.punchline: Mac's summary correctly identifies that everything they've been chasing is based on a fake identity — and then he and Frank calmly confirm: no name, possibly not on Facebook.
jokes.explanation: Good beat that underlines the futility of their quest. Functional plot-comedy rather than a standout joke, but the calm confirmation of total failure is the IASIP style.

jokes.text: Well, how did you find me? Was it that Sally? Because that bitch been getting on my nerves. So you know Sally? Oh, uh, Dylan knows Sally. No, he doesn't, 'cause Dylan isn't real, and you know what? Sally isn't Sally anymore; Sally is now Dylan.
jokes.setup: Mac reveals they found her through Sally; Catfish reveals Sally has now taken on the Dylan Toback persona.
jokes.punchline: The online identity shell game: Dylan was Catfish, now Sally is Dylan — a Ponzi scheme of fake personas.
jokes.explanation: The cascading fake identity reveal is a good structural joke about the internet's unreality. 'Sally is now Dylan' is a funny line because it's delivered matter-of-factly.

jokes.text: And what about the nude photos? I mean... This is not about the nude photos, Mac... Shh! Shh! / Don't you shush me! / Don't you shush us, goddamn it.
jokes.setup: The conversation is about to end; Mac brings up the nude photos; Catfish tries to shush them.
jokes.punchline: Catfish shushes Mac and Frank — the episode's central grievance is replicated exactly by this new character, in this new context.
jokes.explanation: This is a perfect structural callback — the episode's whole engine has been the shushing incident, and now they encounter a new shusher in the least expected context (an elderly catfisher by her husband's life support). 'Don't you shush us, goddamn it!' from Mac and Frank, who have been chasing this exact moment, is enormously satisfying. The structure — finding the shusher they were looking for in an entirely unexpected form — is excellent sitcom writing.

jokes.text: Don't disturb Jerry. / Disturb Jerry? I'm disturbed. / He should be disturbed. / This whole thing is disturbing, and if you shush me one more time I will put you in the ground. Do you hear me?
jokes.setup: Catfish asks them not to disturb Jerry on life support.
jokes.punchline: Frank's existential 'I'm disturbed' and Mac's 'He should be disturbed' (pointing at the man on life support) escalates to Mac threatening to 'put her in the ground' over a shush.
jokes.explanation: The 'disturb Jerry' wordplay — existential disturbance vs. disturbing a comatose man — is a quick three-way escalation. Mac threatening to 'put her in the ground' over a shush is a very dark escalation that pulls together the episode's murder-kit energy from the opening, bringing it full circle.

jokes.text: Let's just get back to the bar, we'll find the nude photos... Oh, yeah, yeah, let's focus on the...
jokes.setup: Mac tries to refocus.
jokes.punchline: Mac says 'let's get back to the bar' and pivots to finding the nude photos — still on that thread despite just having threatened an elderly woman.
jokes.explanation: Mild beat — Mac's consistent interest in the nude photos despite everything else happening is a small irony. Functional.

jokes.text: Don't you want your hair back? / Is that your hair, Dee? / Oh, come on. / You're Carl Lundegard? Yeah.
jokes.setup: The gang is about to leave; Catfish offers 'your hair back' — implying Dee sent hair to this catfisher.
jokes.punchline: Dee has been revealed to have sent hair to the catfish, and her online alias was apparently 'Carl Lundegard' — a male name, suggesting Dee was also catfishing.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Dee sent her hair to the catfish and was going by 'Carl Lundegard' is an excellent delayed reveal. It retroactively recontextualizes Dee's whole subplot (she was pursuing this relationship) and pays off the hair-mailing thread from jokes #54 and #57. 'Carl Lundegard' is a specifically funny male name choice. High character integration: Dee's desperation and self-delusion make this completely believable.

jokes.text: I mean, what is the problem? Are we not putting these in the right part of town? We put them in every part of town...
jokes.setup: Dennis and Charlie's wanted poster plan isn't working.
jokes.punchline: Dennis can't understand why the poster isn't working — his confidence in the plan is unshakeable despite it being objectively absurd.
jokes.explanation: Functional beat — Dennis's unshakeable confidence in a terrible plan is consistent. Not a standout on its own.

jokes.text: Hello? / Saw that guy you were looking for. / You did? / Oh, that's great, okay, can you tell us where exactly the... / Shh! / Uh, no, oh, you do not! Oh! You... ugh! He shushed me.
jokes.setup: Dennis gets a call in response to the wanted poster.
jokes.punchline: The caller shushes Dennis mid-sentence — the poster has attracted shushers who call specifically to shush people.
jokes.explanation: Perfect ironic payoff to the wanted poster plan: by advertising that they're looking for a shusher, they've attracted other shushers who call to shush them. The structure is elegant — the solution has become the problem. 'He shushed me' delivered with fresh outrage despite this being the same grievance is very funny. This is one of the episode's tightest structural jokes.

jokes.text: Another one? Yes, another shusher shushing me on the phone. All right, maybe the poster is the problem because it says 'Rude man who shushes please call...' Right. So rude men are calling just to shush you. This is prank calls. Am I gonna have to change my phone number? I mean, that's... Yes, because you never want to put your personal information out there in the world. It's like... People abuse it.
jokes.setup: Dennis gets shushed by callers responding to the poster.
jokes.punchline: Charlie points out the obvious flaw in the plan; Dennis's earlier speech about 'connecting with people' by putting his info out there is now literally resulting in anonymous shushers calling him.
jokes.explanation: The thematic irony is fully paid off: Dennis advocated for real connection and sharing personal info, now anonymous strangers are shushing him via phone. Charlie's observation 'you never want to put your personal information out there in the world' directly contradicts what Dennis said earlier. Good structural irony that ties the episode's themes together.

jokes.text: No, we just hit a bunch of dead ends, right? The guy is a ghost, I'm telling you. I know! We tried to track him down on Facebook, but it got very strange. Like, it was just a bunch of girls pretending to be boys, and Dee banged a fat old black la[dy], and then sent her hair.
jokes.setup: The gang reconvenes to compare results.
jokes.punchline: Mac's summary reduces their entire adventure to: a bunch of gender-swapped catfish and 'Dee banged a fat old black lady and then sent her hair' — an absurd compression that exposes how ridiculous everything has been.
jokes.explanation: Mac's brutal summary — particularly 'Dee banged a fat old black lady and then sent her hair' — is a great comedic compression of the subplot's absurdity. The specificity makes it funnier than a vague summary.

jokes.text: Hey, I did the video, and I sent it to all of Paddy's Facebook friends. / You did? / Frank to the rescue.
jokes.setup: Everyone has failed at their respective tasks.
jokes.punchline: Frank announces he completed the video and sent it — the gang immediately celebrates before seeing what he actually made.
jokes.explanation: Setup for the virus video payoff. 'Frank to the rescue' as premature celebration is a good beat. The reveal is the real joke; this is the setup.

jokes.text: Welcome to Paddy's Pub... the oldest pub in America. / Well, that's not true. / Right. / No, I lied. Everybody lies on the Internet. / He's right. Everybody out there is lying to get what they want; why can't we?
jokes.setup: Frank's video opens with a false claim.
jokes.punchline: Frank admits the lie immediately; Dennis and Mac decide that since everyone lies on the internet, Paddy's should too — rationalizing dishonesty as internet-normal.
jokes.explanation: The gang's immediate embrace of internet dishonesty ('why can't we?') ties into the episode's catfishing theme. The logic is funny because it's both wrong and correct simultaneously.

jokes.text: We have a variety of old liquors served in strange containers. / We are packed with celebrities — the fun ones. / We also have cockfights and strippers. / And guess what? We don't have a sign, so good luck finding the place. / But if you do, you'll be lucky. 'Cause we also got donkey shows, Motley Crue and cake.
jokes.setup: Frank's promotional video for Paddy's Pub plays.
jokes.punchline: The video escalates from 'old liquors in strange containers' to cockfights, strippers, donkey shows, Motley Crue, and cake — each addition more absurd than the last, with 'cake' as the final random item.
jokes.explanation: Frank's escalating list is one of the episode's best extended jokes. The structure is perfect: each item is funnier than the last ('cockfights' → 'strippers' → 'donkey shows' → 'Motley Crue' → 'cake'). 'Cake' as the final, perfectly mundane item after the depravity is a classic comedy rhythm move. 'The fun ones' as a qualifier for celebrities is a great small joke. This video is the comedic centerpiece of the episode's third act.

jokes.text: So, spread the word to all of your friends: At Paddy's Pub, you're guaranteed to catch a... / Virus! / Just ask this guy. / I got infected. / Get that away from me.
jokes.setup: Frank's video reaches its call-to-action section, asking viewers to 'spread the word'
jokes.punchline: The 'spread the word' call-to-action becomes 'spread a virus' — 'guaranteed to catch a Virus!' — with Mac reluctantly appearing in frame saying 'I got infected' and immediately trying to escape
jokes.explanation: The payoff to Frank's literal-viral misunderstanding from earlier. 'Get that away from me' shows Mac's continuing disgust even as he's in the shot. The structure of the video building to a call-to-action that is literally 'come catch a disease' is well-constructed. Good callback payoff.

jokes.text: So, spread the word to all of your friends: At Paddy's Pub, you're guaranteed to catch a... / Virus! / Just ask this guy. / I got infected. / Get that away from me. / Or her. / No, I'm busy. / She looks like she caught the... / Bug! / So spread this video to all of your friends, because it's a computer virus. / Virus! / Take it from me. I am a doctor... Dr. Toboggan. / Mantis Toboggan.
jokes.setup: Frank's 'viral video' ends with people saying 'virus' and 'bug' and Frank identifying himself as 'Dr. Mantis Toboggan.'
jokes.punchline: Frank thought 'viral video' meant a video about a computer virus. His confusion between 'viral' (marketing) and 'virus' (malware) is the episode's central payoff joke. 'Mantis Toboggan' is an absurdly specific fake doctor name.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best extended joke. The 'viral video' vs. 'virus' confusion has been seeded throughout the episode — Frank kept calling it 'the virus thing' and no one corrected him. The payoff is a video that earnestly promotes Paddy's as a place where you'll 'catch a virus,' with Mac reluctantly saying 'I got infected,' Dee saying 'Bug!' The whole sequence is brilliantly constructed. And then: 'Dr. Mantis Toboggan.' This name is one of the greatest character aliases in IASIP history — 'Mantis' is a meaningless, vaguely menacing first name, and 'Toboggan' is a sled. It's a perfect absurdist construction. This ranks among the best jokes in this episode by every metric: structure (9/10), earned payoff (9/10), originality (8.5/10), and quotability (9.5/10).

jokes.text: Virus! / Take it from me. / I am a doctor... Dr. Toboggan. / Mantis Toboggan.
jokes.setup: Frank's video has a testimonial section featuring Dennis
jokes.punchline: Dennis introduces himself as 'Dr. Toboggan' — then clarifies the full name is 'Mantis Toboggan' — a completely invented doctor name with a first name so absurd it needs a full beat to land
jokes.explanation: The best single joke in the episode and one of the most quotable moments in Always Sunny's run. 'Dr. Toboggan' is already funny — the name is absurd but plausible as a fake medical name. Then the pause and the full reveal: 'Mantis Toboggan.' The first name 'Mantis' is extraordinary — it's not a name, it's a predatory insect, and combined with 'Toboggan' (a sled), the full name is 'Mantis Toboggan, M.D.' The two-beat structure — 'Dr. Toboggan' pause 'Mantis Toboggan' — gives the punchline room to breathe. This became a cultural touchstone for the show. Near-perfect economy (four words for the punchline), exceptional originality.

jokes.text: What? / You sent that to all of our Facebook friends? / Yeah. / They're gonna think they have a computer virus, Frank. / Wait, you're the ones who said we needed the virus video. / I said a 'viral video,' Frank. Goddamn it. Goddamn it!
jokes.setup: The gang watches Frank's completed video.
jokes.punchline: The confirmation: Frank genuinely believed 'viral video' meant 'video about a virus.' Dennis's exasperated 'I said a viral video, Frank. Goddamn it. Goddamn it!' is the button.
jokes.explanation: The reveal of Frank's misunderstanding (which the audience has been waiting for since the 'virus thing' was first mentioned) is fully paid off. Dennis's repeated 'Goddamn it. Goddamn it!' is a perfect frustrated response. The structure — mac told Frank to 'get started and we'll come fix what you did,' and what he did was catastrophically wrong — is satisfying callback to joke #37.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, we never should've left him in charge. / See, the problem is we got focused on the guy. We didn't help him with his... / This whole thing is a total mess. / I mean, absolutely nothing good has come of today.
jokes.setup: The gang assesses the disaster.
jokes.punchline: 'Absolutely nothing good has come of today' is the episode's honest summary — delivered with the deadpan of people who have done this many times.
jokes.explanation: Classic IASIP episode wrap-up — everyone acknowledges failure with zero self-reflection. 'Absolutely nothing good has come of today' is a great summation line. Functional rather than spectacular.

jokes.text: Excuse me. This is a bar, right? We noticed you guys didn't have a sign out front. Thought that was pretty cool. / You guys open? / Yes, we are. / Charlie, lock the door.
jokes.setup: The gang has concluded the whole day was a waste. The sign is still missing (Charlie removed it in joke #12).
jokes.punchline: New customers arrive specifically because there's no sign — validating Frank's theory about exclusivity that the gang mocked all episode. Dennis immediately locks the door to keep it exclusive.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best structural moment and a genuinely excellent sitcom tag. Everything comes together: Charlie accidentally created the exclusivity they needed by literally removing the sign; Frank's theory (which everyone mocked) is proven correct; and Dennis's response — 'Charlie, lock the door' — immediately tries to weaponize the exclusivity. The structure scores 9.5 because it ties together the sign gag (jokes #1, #6, #7, #8, #12, #13), Frank's theory (jokes #10, #11), and the viral video plan (all episode) in a single, wordless moment of irony. 'Charlie, lock the door' is the perfect button — their instinct is immediately to gate-keep the success. Comparable to the best episode-closer callbacks in classic sitcom writing.

jokes.text: This is a bar, right? We noticed you guys didn't have a sign out front. Thought that was pretty cool. / You guys open? / Yes, we are. / Charlie, lock the door.
jokes.setup: Customers walk in because they were attracted by the missing sign — the exact exclusivity-without-a-sign marketing that Frank insisted on all episode
jokes.punchline: Frank's dumb strategy actually worked — but Dennis's response is to lock the door, keeping the customers out or in (ambiguously). The sign-removing plot pays off exactly as Frank predicted, and the gang can't even process it.
jokes.explanation: The episode's best structural joke and a perfect callback to the opening. Frank was right — the sign-less bar IS attractive — but it took all episode and a web of catfishing to get here. Dennis's instinctive 'Charlie, lock the door' instead of welcoming the customers suggests they can't function even when they win. The payoff to the sign joke that opened the episode, landing in the final 30 seconds, is excellent sitcom construction. The ambiguity of whether locking the door means trapping customers or excluding them adds a final dark note.

tmdb_overview: The gang uses the Internet to cyber-stalk their prey. Frank tries to drum up business for Paddy's with a viral video.
